questions.question: What does the multiplication rule state for events $A$ and $B$ with $P(A)>0$?
options: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)P(B)$
$P(A\mid B)=P(A)+P(B)$
$P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A)$
$P(A^c)=P(A)P(B)$

questions.question: For independent events, what happens to the conditional factor in the multiplication rule?
options: It becomes zero for every event
It reduces to the marginal probability
It becomes the probability of the complement event
It must be larger than one

questions.question: A customer clicks an ad with probability $0.1$ and buys with probability $0.3$ given click. What is the probability of click and buy?
Why is the multiplication rule not the same as assuming independence?
options: It can only be used for disjoint events
The conditional factor may differ from the marginal probability
It never includes conditional probability
It applies only when all the events involved have equal probabilities

questions.question: Two cards are drawn without replacement. What expression gives the probability both are aces?
If $P(A\cap B)=0.18$ and $P(A)=0.6$, what is $P(B\mid A)$?
Why does the multiplication rule $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A)$ require $P(A)>0$?
options: because the rule only holds when $B$ is independent of $A$
because the rule gives a wrong value for $P(A\cap B)$ when $P(A)=0$
because $P(B\mid A)=P(A\cap B)/P(A)$ is undefined when $P(A)=0$
because the rule divides $P(A\cap B)$ by $P(B)$, which must be positive

questions.question: Suppose $\mathbb{P}(A\cap B\cap C)>0$. The chain rule is applied to $\mathbb{P}(A\cap B\cap C)$ once in the order $A,B,C$ and once in the order $C,B,A$. Which statement is correct?
options: The two products are equal, although the individual factors may differ
The two products are equal, and their factors agree one by one
The two products may differ, because the order of conditioning matters
Only the order $A,B,C$ is valid, because events must be taken as listed

questions.question: A menu has $3$ starters, $4$ main courses and $2$ desserts. A meal consists of one starter, one main course and one dessert. How many different meals are possible?
For which two-stage procedure is the number of outcomes NOT given by a single product $a\cdot b$ of the stage counts?
options: Choose a chair from $10$ people, then a different person as secretary
Roll a die, then toss a coin
Roll a die; toss one coin if it is even, two coins if it is odd
Pick two different letters of the alphabet, in order

questions.question: Let $A_1,A_2,A_3$ be events with $\mathbb{P}(A_1\cap A_2)>0$. Which expression always equals $\mathbb{P}(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)$?
options: $\mathbb{P}(A_1)\,\mathbb{P}(A_2\mid A_1)\,\mathbb{P}(A_3\mid A_1\cap A_2)$
$\mathbb{P}(A_1)\,\mathbb{P}(A_2\mid A_1)\,\mathbb{P}(A_3\mid A_2)$
$\mathbb{P}(A_1)\,\mathbb{P}(A_2)\,\mathbb{P}(A_3)$
$\mathbb{P}(A_1)\,\mathbb{P}(A_2\mid A_1)\,\mathbb{P}(A_3\mid A_1)$
